export const meta = {
  name: 'probe-schedule-test12',
  description: 'Black-box characterize test12_executable across argparse + schedule dimensions',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Probe', detail: 'six parallel probe agents run the executable' },
    { title: 'Synthesize', detail: 'merge findings into one implementation spec' },
  ],
}

const COMMON = `
You are black-box characterizing a PyInstaller executable: /workspace/dataset/test12_executable
Its Python source is /workspace/dataset/test12.py (short; you MAY read it). It uses argparse (--a/--b/--c, type=int, all required)
and the \`schedule\` library, printing job intervals and Job() reprs.

HARD RULES:
- Do NOT extract, unpack, decompile, or run \`strings\`/binwalk/pyi-archive_viewer on the executable, and do NOT try to read the
  bundled \`schedule\` package source. Characterize by RUNNING it only. This is a strict black-box exercise.
- ALWAYS wrap every run in \`timeout 8\` (some inputs loop forever / for minutes). Never run the executable without a timeout.
  Passing 0 to --a/--b/--c hangs forever; -1 to --a or --b takes ~1min+. Budget accordingly and note timeouts as such.
- Capture stdout and stderr SEPARATELY and record the exit code, e.g.:
    timeout 8 /workspace/dataset/test12_executable --a 5 --b 10 --c 3 >/tmp/o 2>/tmp/e; echo "rc=$?"; echo "--out--"; cat -A /tmp/o; echo "--err--"; cat -A /tmp/e
  Use \`cat -A\` whenever exact spaces/tabs/newlines matter (report the real characters, not the $ markers, in your answer).
- Report EXACT byte-level text: leading/trailing spaces, blank lines, punctuation.

BASELINE (already established, do not re-derive):
  --a 5 --b 10 --c 3  ->  rc=0, stdout:
5
10
3
Job(interval=1, unit=days, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})   (x8 more weeks lines, 9 Job lines total)
12
`

const SPEC_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  additionalProperties: false,
  required: ['dimension', 'rules', 'cases', 'gotchas'],
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    rules: {
      type: 'array',
      description: 'Precise, implementable rules inferred (imperative, unambiguous). Include exact format strings.',
      items: { type: 'string' },
    },
    cases: {
      type: 'array',
      description: 'Concrete observed cases, verbatim output.',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        additionalProperties: false,
        required: ['args', 'exitCode', 'stdout', 'stderr'],
        properties: {
          args: { type: 'string', description: 'Argv after the program name, shell-quoted' },
          exitCode: { type: 'integer', description: 'Exit code; use 124 for timeout' },
          stdout: { type: 'string' },
          stderr: { type: 'string' },
          note: { type: 'string' },
        },
      },
    },
    gotchas: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
}

const PROBES = [
  {
    key: 'int-parsing',
    prompt: `${COMMON}
DIMENSION: exactly which strings argparse's \`type=int\` accepts / rejects, and the exact rejection message.
Hold --b and --c at valid values (e.g. --b 1 --c 1) and vary --a. Determine acceptance and the parsed value.
Test at minimum: "5", "  5  ", "\\t5\\n", "+5", "-5", "007", "+007", "1_000", "1_0_0", "1__0", "_1", "1_", "-_1", "0x10", "0b101",
"0o17", "1e3", "1.0", "1.", ".5", "", " ", "5 5", "1,000", "inf", "nan", "None", "true", "5x", "x5", "٥" (U+0665 Arabic-Indic five),
"٥٦", "５" (U+FF15 fullwidth five), "５６", "१२" (Devanagari), "𝟝" (U+1D7DD math double-struck five), "²" (superscript two),
"½", "Ⅴ" (Roman numeral), "5\\u00a0" (nbsp), "\\u20035" (en-quad + 5), "-0", "+0" (NOTE: 0 hangs — use timeout and report rc=124),
"０" (fullwidth zero, also hangs).
For each: does it parse, to what value (read it off stdout line 1), or what is the exact stderr text?
Report the exact invalid-value message format (quoting style around the value, and how weird characters are shown).
Also: is the message repr()-style (e.g. does '\\t5' show as '\\t5')? Test that specifically.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'option-syntax',
    prompt: `${COMMON}
DIMENSION: argparse option-string syntax and error behavior.
Test at minimum: --a=5 form; -a 5; -a5; --a5; --ab 5; --A 5; -- separator ("--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --" and "-- --a 1 ...");
repeated options (last wins?); options out of order; a bare positional ("foo --a 1 --b 2 --c 3" and "--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 foo");
two unrecognized args at once; "--a" with no value; "--a --b 2 --c 3"; "--a -5" (negative value); "--a=-5";
"--a=" (empty after equals); "--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 extra1 extra2"; "-abc"; "---a 5"; "--a 1 -b 2 --c 3".
Record exact usage/error lines, which stream they go to, and exit codes.
Determine: what is the exact "unrecognized arguments" message when multiple extras exist (separator/order)?
What is the exact "expected one argument" message? What is the exact missing-required message and the ORDER of listed args
(test omitting different subsets: only --a given, only --b given, only --c given, only --a and --c given, none given)?`,
  },
  {
    key: 'help-usage',
    prompt: `${COMMON}
DIMENSION: help and usage text, byte-exact.
Capture: -h, --help, --he, --h, --hel, and -h combined with other args ("-h --a 1", "--a 1 -h", "--a bad -h", "-h --zzz").
Which stream, exact bytes (use cat -A to see trailing spaces), exit codes.
Also determine whether terminal width affects wrapping: run with COLUMNS=20 and COLUMNS=200 exported (and note whether
COLUMNS is even honored when stdout is a pipe). Report the exact help text including the blank line placement and the
indentation of the options block (count spaces precisely).
Also: does the header say "options:" or "optional arguments:"?`,
  },
  {
    key: 'schedule-repr',
    prompt: `${COMMON}
DIMENSION: the printed Job() repr and job bookkeeping.
Confirm byte-exactly all 9 Job lines and the final job count. Then determine how the printed \`interval\` (first three lines)
and the repr interval relate to inputs. Vary --a/--b/--c over valid positive values including 1, 2, 7, 60, 3600, 86400,
1000000, 2147483647, 2147483648, 4294967296, 250000000000, and a value with many digits like 12345678901234567890 (expect an
error there — record it). Confirm the first three stdout lines are exactly the three integers as Python prints them
(no separators, no sign for positives, "+5" input printed as 5).
Also confirm the count line is always 12 whenever the program completes, and that stdout lines appear in source order,
with prints interleaved before any later failure (e.g. --a 5 --b 5 --c <bad> still prints 5 and 5 first).`,
  },
  {
    key: 'overflow-map',
    prompt: `${COMMON}
DIMENSION: overflow / error surface for large and negative intervals, per unit.
Units: --a is seconds (source line 11), --b is minutes (line 13), --c is hours (line 15).
Already known:
  --a 100000000000000 -> rc=1, stderr traceback, deepest frame "schedule/__init__.py", line 729, in _schedule_next_run,
     OverflowError: days=1157407407; must have magnitude <= 999999999
  --a 86400000000000 -> same shape, "days=1000000000; must have magnitude <= 999999999"
  --a 12345678901234567890... very large -> line 729, OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C int
  --a 300000000000 -> line 731, OverflowError: date value out of range
  --a 250000000000 and 251000000000 -> rc=0 (no overflow)
  --c 2147483647 -> line 731, date value out of range;  --c -1 -> line 734, date value out of range (~1s)
YOUR JOB: pin down the EXACT thresholds by bisection for the seconds unit (--a) between the three regimes:
  (A) rc=0, (B) line 731 "date value out of range", (C) line 729 "days=N; must have magnitude <= 999999999",
  (D) line 729 "Python int too large to convert to C int".
Report the largest --a with rc=0 and the smallest --a giving regime B; the smallest giving C; the smallest giving D.
Do the same for --c (hours): largest rc=0 value and smallest overflow value. And for --b (minutes): find the smallest
positive value that overflows (bisect; it should be large).
Also test NEGATIVE large magnitudes: --a -100000000000000, --a -12345678901234567890, --c -2147483647, --c -1000000,
--c -100000, --c -24, --c -1000 (which of these error immediately at 729 vs 731 vs 734, and what message?).
Note: the threshold for regime B depends on TODAY'S DATE (it is now 2026-08-10) since it is "now + period > datetime.max".
State the rule in date terms, not just the raw number. Give the exact full traceback text (all 5 lines) for one example of
each regime, and note that the final "[PYI-NNN:ERROR] ..." line's number varies per run (report whether it equals the PID).`,
  },
  {
    key: 'loop-scaling',
    prompt: `${COMMON}
DIMENSION: confirm the negative/zero interval behavior is a linear step loop, and measure its scaling.
Hypothesis: schedule computes next_run = now + period, then runs \`while next_run <= now: next_run += period\` (line 734),
so period==0 loops forever and period<0 walks backwards until the datetime underflows year 1 -> OverflowError: date value out of range.
Verify by timing (use \`time timeout N ...\`, N sized per case):
  --c -1 (hours), --c -2, --c -4, --c -24, --c -168  (expect time roughly proportional to 1/|interval|)
  --a -3600 (seconds, one hour per step) should take about the same wall time as --c -1 (hours).
  --a -86400 vs --c -24 should match too.
Also confirm: --a 0 / --b 0 / --c 0 never terminate (run with timeout 10, report rc=124 and empty output), and confirm
whether ANY stdout was produced before the hang (e.g. --a 5 --b 5 --c 0 should print 5 and 5 first — check whether those
bytes actually appear when stdout is a pipe vs when it is a tty; note Python block-buffers a piped stdout, so report both).
Use \`script -qc\` or a pty if needed to test the tty case; if you cannot, say so.
Report a table of |interval| vs wall seconds, and state whether the linear-loop hypothesis holds.`,
  },
]

phase('Probe')
const results = await parallel(
  PROBES.map((p) => () => agent(p.prompt, { label: `probe:${p.key}`, phase: 'Probe', schema: SPEC_SCHEMA, effort: 'high' }))
)

const good = results.filter(Boolean)
log(`${good.length}/${PROBES.length} probes returned`)

phase('Synthesize')
const spec = await agent(
  `You are consolidating black-box probe results for a Python->Node.js migration of /workspace/dataset/test12.py
(argparse with --a/--b/--c type=int required, plus the \`schedule\` library).

Here are the raw probe reports as JSON:

${JSON.stringify(good, null, 2)}

Produce a single precise IMPLEMENTATION SPEC in markdown for a Node.js (ESM) reimplementation with zero dependencies.
It must state, unambiguously and byte-exactly:
1. Argument parsing: accepted syntaxes, the int() grammar (whitespace/sign/underscore/unicode-digit rules), and every
   error message template with exact wording, stream, and exit code. Include the missing-required-argument ordering rule.
2. The exact usage line and full help text.
3. The normal-path stdout, line by line, and the Job repr template.
4. The complete error/overflow model: timedelta construction limits and messages, datetime range overflow, the
   while-loop semantics (zero -> non-terminating, negative -> walk back to year 1 -> OverflowError), and the exact
   traceback text per regime including the schedule/__init__.py line numbers (729 / 731 / 734) and test12.py line numbers
   (11 / 13 / 15) and the trailing PyInstaller line.
5. Any contradictions or gaps between probe reports — call them out explicitly under "## UNRESOLVED" rather than papering over them.
Be exhaustive but do not invent anything the probes did not observe. Quote exact strings in fenced blocks.`,
  { label: 'synthesize-spec', phase: 'Synthesize', effort: 'high' }
)

return spec
result:
# IMPLEMENTATION SPEC — Node.js (ESM, zero dependencies) reimplementation of `/workspace/dataset/test12.py`

Reference binary: `/workspace/dataset/test12_executable` (PyInstaller onefile freeze of `/workspace/dataset/test12.py`).
Source (read, 39 lines) — the line numbers that appear in tracebacks are load-bearing:

| source line | statement |
|---|---|
| 11 | `job1 = schedule.every(args.a).seconds.do(lambda: None)` |
| 12 | `print(job1.interval)` |
| 13 | `job2 = schedule.every(args.b).minutes.do(lambda: None)` |
| 14 | `print(job2.interval)` |
| 15 | `job3 = schedule.every(args.c).hours.do(lambda: None)` |
| 16 | `print(job3.interval)` |
| 19–36 | `job4..job12` = `.day`, `.week`, `.monday`…`.sunday`, each followed by `print(jobN)` |
| 38–39 | `all_jobs = schedule.get_jobs()` / `print(len(all_jobs))` |

Everything below is either **[OBSERVED]** (directly in a probe case), **[RULE]** (probe-asserted rule consistent across reports), or **[INFERRED]** (logically required to fill a gap the probes did not execute — all such items are also listed under `## UNRESOLVED`).

---

## 1. Process shape, streams, exit codes

### 1.1 PROG name
Every usage/error line is prefixed with `PROG` = **basename of argv[0]** (the invoked program path), *not* a hardcoded string. **[OBSERVED]** invoking through a symlink `/tmp/zzz-prog` produced `usage: zzz-prog …` / `zzz-prog: error: …`. In normal runs PROG is `test12_executable`.

Node: derive PROG from the launch path the wrapper is invoked as (e.g. `basename(process.argv[1])` for a `node script.js` layout, or `basename(process.argv[0])` for a packaged binary). It MUST be `test12_executable` when the artifact is named that.

### 1.2 Exit codes
| code | condition |
|---|---|
| `0` | success (13 stdout lines) **or** `-h`/`--help` |
| `2` | any argparse error (all four templates) |
| `1` | runtime `OverflowError` from `schedule` (positive-overflow tiers *and* negative intervals) |
| *(none)* | `0` for any of `--a/--b/--c` → process never terminates (harness observes `124` under `timeout`) |

`124` is never a program exit code — it is `timeout`'s kill. **[RULE]**

### 1.3 Stream discipline and buffering
- All argparse output on error goes **entirely to stderr**; stdout is **empty** (0 bytes) — argparse runs before any `print`. **[RULE]**
- Help goes to **stdout**, rc 0, stderr empty. **[OBSERVED]**
- Success output goes to stdout, stderr **exactly 0 bytes**. **[OBSERVED]**
- Every line is LF-terminated. No CR, no trailing blank line, no trailing spaces (single documented exception: `unrecognized arguments: ` with an empty-string extra), no leading/trailing whitespace on any line. **[RULE]**
- **Buffering emulation (required for behavioural parity):** the reference is CPython, so stdout is *block-buffered when redirected to a file/pipe* and *line-buffered on a TTY*. Consequences that a Node port must reproduce:
  - Non-TTY + infinite hang (`0` interval) ⇒ **empty stdout**, empty stderr, forever. **[OBSERVED]** (`--a 5 --b 0 --c 1` → rc 124, empty stdout; under a pty the same run shows `5`.)
  - TTY + infinite hang ⇒ the pre-hang lines DO appear (`--a 5 --b 7 --c 0` under `script -qefc` produced `5\r\n7\r\n`; the `\r` is the pty, not the program). **[OBSERVED]**
  - Crash paths (rc 1) **do** flush everything printed before the exception, even to a file — CPython flushes std streams at interpreter shutdown. **[OBSERVED]** (`--a 5 --b 10 --c -168` → stdout `5\n10\n` in a redirected file.)
  - `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` does **not** change this (the PyInstaller bootloader ignores it). **[RULE]** Do not make the Node port honour it either.

  Implementation: accumulate stdout in an in-memory buffer and flush on normal exit / before printing a traceback when `!process.stdout.isTTY`; write immediately per line when `process.stdout.isTTY`.

---

## 2. Argument parsing (argparse, `--a/--b/--c`, `type=int`, all `required=True`)

### 2.1 Accepted option syntax
Long form only, two spellings, exactly equivalent: **[RULE]**

```
--a VALUE      --a=VALUE
--b VALUE      --b=VALUE
--c VALUE      --c=VALUE
-h  --help
```

There are **no** single-dash aliases and **no** attached-value form. All of the following are unknown options: `-a`, `-a5`, `-abc`, `--a5`, `--ab`, `--A` (names are case-sensitive), `---a`. **[OBSERVED]**

Option order on the command line is irrelevant; a repeated option silently keeps the **last** value with no warning (`--a 1 --a 7` → `7`) — store action, no append. **[OBSERVED]**

Spaces around `=` are not allowed: `--a = 5` makes `=` the value of `--a`. **[OBSERVED]**

`--a=` supplies the **empty string** (an invalid int), which is a *different* error from a bare trailing `--a` (missing value). **[OBSERVED]**

### 2.2 Is a `-`-prefixed token an option or a value?
Reproduce argparse's negative-number heuristic. Because this parser declares no option string that looks like a negative number, `-`-prefixed numeric tokens are treated as **values**: **[RULE]**

- token `"-"` (lone dash) → **not** an option; it becomes a leftover extra. **[OBSERVED]** (`unrecognized arguments: -`)
- token matching `/^-\d+$/` or `/^-\d*\.\d+$/` → **value**. **[OBSERVED]** `--a -5` and `--a=-5` both feed `-5` to `int()`; the only complaint in `--a -5 --b 2` is the missing `--c`, never "expected one argument".
- any other `-`-prefixed token → **option-like**, so it is NOT consumed as a value. **[OBSERVED]** `--a -_1` yields `argument --a: expected one argument`, *not* `invalid int value`, because `int()` is never called.
- CPython additionally treats a `-`-prefixed token containing a space as a positional. **[INFERRED]** (not probed)

### 2.3 `--` separator
Observed behaviour, to be copied literally: **[OBSERVED]**
- Tokens after the first `--` are not parsed as options.
- The `--` itself is **not** stripped (the parser declares no positionals, so nothing consumes it) and appears in the extras list:
  - `--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --` → `unrecognized arguments: --`
  - `--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 -- foo bar` → `unrecognized arguments: -- foo bar`
- But when a required option ends up missing, extras are suppressed by precedence (§2.6):
  - `-- --a 1 --b 2 --c 3` → `the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c`
  - `--a 1 -- --b 2 --c 3` → `the following arguments are required: --b, --c`
  - `--` alone → `the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c`

### 2.4 The `int()` grammar (value conversion)

Acceptance is **exactly CPython `int(str)`**, base 10. argparse layers nothing on top: no range check, no `>= 0` check, no float fallback. **[RULE]**

Accepted grammar:

```
value  := WS* SIGN? DIGITS WS*
SIGN   := "+" | "-"                     ; ASCII only
DIGITS := D ( "_" D )*   where D := digit+
digit  := any code point with Unicode General_Category = Nd
WS     := any code point Python considers whitespace (see below)
```

Normative details:
- **Leading zeros allowed and ignored:** `007`→7, `+007`→7, `00`→0, `010`→10. **[OBSERVED]**
- **Sign:** ASCII `+`/`-` only. `U+2212 MINUS SIGN` is rejected. No space between sign and digits (`+ 5` rejected). **[OBSERVED]**
- **PEP 515 underscores:** single separators strictly *between* digits. `1_000`→1000, `1_0_0`→100 accepted; `1__0`, `_1`, `1_` rejected. **[OBSERVED]**
- **Unicode digits:** every `Nd` code point is accepted and mixes freely with ASCII, valued positionally:
  `٥`(U+0665)→5, `٥٦`→56, `５`(U+FF15)→5, `５６`→56, `१२`→12, `U+1D7DD`(astral)→5, `1٥`→15, `０`(U+FF10)→0. **[OBSERVED]**
- **Non-`Nd` numerics are REJECTED** even though they have numeric value: `²`(No), `½`(No), `Ⅴ`/`Ⅵ`(Nl). Do **not** use "has a numeric value" as the test. **[RULE]**
- **Whitespace stripped, leading AND trailing, any quantity/mixture.** Confirmed-strippable: space, `\t`(U+0009), `\n`(U+000A), `\v`(U+000B), `\f`(U+000C), `\r`(U+000D), NBSP(U+00A0), U+1680, U+2000, U+2003, U+3000. **[OBSERVED]** `U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE` is **NOT** whitespace and is rejected. **[OBSERVED]**
  CPython's full `Py_UNICODE_ISSPACE` set additionally contains U+001C–U+001F, U+0085, U+2001–U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F. **[INFERRED]** — implement the full set; only the list above is probe-verified.
- **Rejected** (non-exhaustive, all probe-verified): base prefixes `0x10`/`0b101`/`0o17`; float syntax `1e3`, `1.0`, `1.`, `.5`, `1.5`, `3.0`; empty `''`; whitespace-only `' '`; embedded space `5 5`; `+ 5`; thousands comma `1,000`; `inf`; `nan`; `None`; `true`; `5x`; `x5`; `=`; `\u200b5`; undecodable argv byte `0xFF`. **[OBSERVED]**
- **Arbitrary precision:** Python ints are unbounded, so `12345678901234567890` and `10000000000000000000000000` are *accepted* by argparse and fail later. Use **BigInt** in Node; never `Number`. **[RULE]**

### 2.5 The four error message templates

Every argparse error is **exactly two lines on stderr**, stdout empty, rc 2: **[RULE]**

```
usage: PROG [-h] --a A --b B --c C
PROG: error: <detail>
```

Detail templates:

**(a) Missing value**
```
argument <OPT>: expected one argument
```
Singular "one argument". `<OPT>` is the long option *with* dashes (`--a`, `--b`, `--c`). Triggered when the option is the last token in argv, or when the next token is option-like (`--a --b 2 --c 3`, `--a -_1`), including a dangling repeat after a good value (`--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --a`). **[OBSERVED]**

**(b) Bad int**
```
argument <OPT>: invalid int value: <REPR>
```
`<REPR>` is **Python `repr()`** of the offending string — see §2.7. It is NOT hand-quoted. Full format string: `{prog}: error: argument {flag}: invalid int value: {value!r}`. **[RULE]**

**(c) Missing required options**
```
the following arguments are required: <LIST>
```
`<LIST>` = the missing option strings joined by `", "` (comma + one space), **always in declaration order `--a, --b, --c`**, regardless of command-line order, with no trailing punctuation. Exhaustive table: **[OBSERVED]**

| given | LIST |
|---|---|
| none | `--a, --b, --c` |
| `--a` only | `--b, --c` |
| `--b` only | `--a, --c` |
| `--c` only | `--a, --b` |
| `--a`+`--c` | `--b` |
| `--b`+`--c` | `--a` |
| `--a`+`--b` | `--c` |

**(d) Unrecognized arguments**
```
unrecognized arguments: <EXTRAS>
```
`<EXTRAS>` = all leftover tokens joined by a **single space**, in left-to-right command-line order, with option-consumed tokens removed. An unknown option and its would-be value are two separate leftovers (`--d 4` → `--d 4`); the `=` form stays one token (`--d=4`). Interleaved extras keep their relative order (`extra1 --a 1 extra2 --b 2 --c 3` → `extra1 extra2`). The empty string contributes nothing but still gets its separator: **[OBSERVED]**
```
unrecognized arguments: 
```
(trailing space before `\n`; verified with `cat -A` as `arguments: $`), and combined with another extra:
```
unrecognized arguments:  foo
```
(two spaces).

### 2.6 Error precedence — the biggest gotcha
Process in this order; the first firing error is the **only** thing printed: **[RULE]**

1. `-h`/`--help` short-circuits → help to stdout, rc 0, **even alongside otherwise-valid options** (`--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --help` prints only help; no job output).
2. `argument <OPT>: expected one argument`
3. `argument <OPT>: invalid int value: <REPR>`
4. `the following arguments are required: …`
5. `unrecognized arguments: …`

Therefore **unrecognized arguments are reported only if all three required options parsed successfully.** `-a 5 -b 10 -c 3`, `-a5 -b10 -c3`, `--a5 --b10 --c3`, `-abc`, `--ab 5 --b 10 --c 3`, `--A 5 --b 10 --c 3`, `---a 5 --b 2 --c 3`, `--a 1 -b 2 --c 3`, `--a 1 --b 2 extra` all emit a *missing-required* error and never mention the unrecognized tokens. **[OBSERVED]**

Within (2)/(3), conversion happens during the single left-to-right pass, so the leftmost failing option is reported (`--a 1 --b abc --c 1` → `argument --b: …`). **[OBSERVED, partially — see UNRESOLVED #6]**

### 2.7 `repr()` rendering of the offending value (required for template (b))

Implement Python `repr()` for `str` exactly: **[RULE]**

1. Quote choice: default `'`. If the string contains `'` and does **not** contain `"`, use `"` instead. If it contains **both**, use `'` and backslash-escape each `'`.
2. Escapes always applied: `\\` for a literal backslash, `\t`, `\n`, `\r`, and the chosen quote when it must be escaped.
3. Every other code point: emitted **raw** if Python's `str.isprintable()` is true, otherwise escaped as `\xNN` (cp < 0x100), `\uNNNN` (cp < 0x10000), or `\UNNNNNNNN` (astral), with **lowercase hex**.
   `str.isprintable()` is false for categories `Cc, Cf, Cs, Co, Cn, Zl, Zp, Zs` — except `U+0020 SPACE`, which is printable and emitted raw.

Verified consequences: **[OBSERVED]**

```
--a 1__0     -> test12_executable: error: argument --a: invalid int value: '1__0'
--a ''       -> ... invalid int value: ''
--a ' '      -> ... invalid int value: ' '            (real 0x20 byte, not \x20)
--a '5 5'    -> ... invalid int value: '5 5'
--a $'\t5x'  -> ... invalid int value: '\t5x'         (two ASCII chars backslash+t)
--a $'a\nb'  -> ... invalid int value: 'a\nb'         (message stays ONE physical line)
--a "5'x"    -> ... invalid int value: "5'x"          (QUOTE SWITCHES to double)
--a "5'\"x"  -> ... invalid int value: '5\'"x'        (both quotes -> escape the apostrophe)
--a '5\x'    -> ... invalid int value: '5\\x'         (one backslash prints as two)
5 + NBSP + X -> ... invalid int value: '5\xa0X'       (U+00A0 not printable -> escaped)
²            -> ... invalid int value: '²'            (printable -> RAW UTF-8 C2 B2)
½            -> ... invalid int value: '½'            (raw C2 BD)
Ⅴ            -> ... invalid int value: 'Ⅴ'            (raw E2 85 A4)
U+2212 + 5   -> ... invalid int value: '−5'           (raw E2 88 92)
U+200B + 5   -> ... invalid int value: '\u200b5'      (non-printable -> escaped, lowercase)
5 + 0xFF     -> ... invalid int value: '5\udcff'      (surrogateescape of undecodable argv byte)
```

The NBSP pair is the most surprising: **U+00A0 is simultaneously strippable whitespace for `int()` and `\x`-escaped in the error message**, while U+00B2 (`²`) is rejected and printed raw. **[RULE]**

Any implementation that hardcodes `'{}'` around the value diverges. **[RULE]**

---

## 3. Usage line and full help text

Usage line (used in every error block, and as line 1 of help):
```
usage: test12_executable [-h] --a A --b B --c C
```

Full help, emitted for `-h` or `--help` anywhere in argv, to **stdout**, rc 0, nothing else printed, stderr empty: **[OBSERVED]**

```
usage: test12_executable [-h] --a A --b B --c C

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
  --a A
  --b B
  --c C
```

Byte-exact form: `usage: …\n` `\n` `options:\n` `  -h, --help  show this help message and exit\n` `  --a A\n` `  --b B\n` `  --c C\n`.
Notes: blank line after usage; Python ≥3.10 header `options:` (not `optional arguments:`); two-space indent; `-h, --help` padded with two spaces so the help text starts at column 15; `--a A`/`--b B`/`--c C` carry **no** help text. **[RULE]**

---

## 4. Normal path stdout (rc 0)

Exactly **13 LF-terminated lines**, stderr 0 bytes, single trailing newline, no trailing blank line: **[RULE]**

```
<str(a)>
<str(b)>
<str(c)>
Job(interval=1, unit=days, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
Job(interval=1, unit=weeks, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
12
```

- **Lines 1–3** are `print(int)` of the parsed `--a`, `--b`, `--c` in **declaration order a, b, c**, regardless of command-line order. Decimal digits only, no thousands separators, no `+`, no leading zeros, arbitrary precision preserved. Normalization examples: `+5`→`5`, `010`→`10`, `1_000`→`1000`, `' 7 '`→`7`, `５`→`5`, `٥٦`→`56`, `251615000000`→`251615000000`. **[OBSERVED]**
- **Line 4** is byte-exactly the `.day` job (`unit=days`).
- **Lines 5–12** are 8 byte-identical `unit=weeks` lines: `.week` **plus** the seven weekday accessors. Count of `weeks` lines is **8, not 7**; total Job lines = **9** = 1 `days` + 8 `weeks`. **[RULE]**
- **The nine Job reprs are constants** — `interval=1` always, unit always `days`/`weeks`. They never reflect `--a/--b/--c`. Verified across a/b/c ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 60, 3600, 86400, 1000000, 69893000, 4193598000, 251615000000}. An implementation that echoes a/b/c into the reprs is wrong. **[RULE]**
- **Job repr template** (no `next_run`, no `at`, no `tags`, no module qualifier, no memory address):
  ```
  Job(interval=<int>, unit=<unit>, do=<lambda>, args=(), kwargs={})
  ```
  prefix `Job(`, fields in order `interval, unit, do, args, kwargs`, separator `, ` (comma + exactly one space), **no spaces around `=`**, `do=<lambda>` (the plain function `__name__` in angle brackets), `args=()` empty tuple literal, `kwargs={}` empty dict literal, closing `)`.
- **Line 13** is always exactly `12` on completion — a process-global `schedule.get_jobs()` count. It never varies with input and is never partial: either `12`, or the program died earlier and the line is absent. **[RULE]**
- **Interleaving is strict source order.** `print(jobN.interval)` follows the `.do()` call, so a failure inside `schedule.every(a).seconds.do(...)` (line 11) means line 1 was never printed. `--a 5 --b 5 --c <overflowing>` emits `5\n5\n` on stdout, then the traceback on stderr. **[OBSERVED]**

---

## 5. Runtime error / overflow model (`schedule`)

`schedule.every(N).<unit>.do(f)` → `Job.do()` (`schedule/__init__.py` line 657) → `Job._schedule_next_run()`. Three distinct source lines inside `_schedule_next_run` raise, and each maps to a distinct regime: **[RULE, line numbers OBSERVED]**

| schedule line | operation (inferred) | raises |
|---|---|---|
| 729 | construct `datetime.timedelta(**{unit: interval})` | `days=<D>; must have magnitude <= 999999999` / `Python int too large to convert to C int` |
| 731 | `next_run = datetime.now() + period` | `date value out of range` (forward overflow past `datetime.max`) |
| 734 | `while next_run <= now: next_run += period` | `date value out of range` (negative period walks back past `datetime.min`) |

Unit map: `--a` → seconds (source line 11), `--b` → minutes (line 13), `--c` → hours (line 15). Let **D = trunc(interval converted to days)** = `a/86400`, `b/1440`, `c/24`. **[RULE]**

### 5.1 Decision procedure per option (evaluate for a, then b, then c, in source order, printing lines 1/2/3 after each success)

```
1. if |D| >= 2**31                       -> TIER 3, schedule line 729
2. else if |D| >= 1_000_000_000          -> TIER 2, schedule line 729
3. else if now + period > datetime.max   -> TIER 1, schedule line 731
   (or, for negative period, now + period < datetime.min)   [INFERRED for the negative side]
4. else if interval == 0                 -> NON-TERMINATING loop at schedule line 734
5. else if interval < 0                  -> TIER 4, schedule line 734 (after ~ (now - datetime.min)/|period| iterations)
6. else                                  -> success, print str(interval)
```

### 5.2 Tier 3 — `Python int too large to convert to C int` (schedule line 729)
Exact, time-independent thresholds (= `2**31 × unit-seconds-per-day-divisor`): **[OBSERVED]**

| option | threshold |
|---|---|
| `--a` | `>= 185542587187200` (= 2³¹ × 86400) |
| `--b` | `>= 3092376453120` (= 2³¹ × 1440) |
| `--c` | `>= 51539607552` (= 2³¹ × 24) |

Off-by-one verified: `--a 185542587187199` → Tier 2 (`days=2147483647`); `--a 185542587187200` → Tier 3. Also hit by `--a 12345678901234567890`, `--a 10000000000000000000000000`, and `--c 250000000000`. Message:
```
OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C int
```

### 5.3 Tier 2 — `days=<D>; must have magnitude <= 999999999` (schedule line 729)
Exact, time-independent thresholds: **[OBSERVED]**

| option | threshold |
|---|---|
| `--a` | `>= 86400000000000` |
| `--b` | `>= 1440000000000` |
| `--c` | `>= 24000000000` |

`<D>` is the **truncated integer day count** and varies with the input: `--a 86400000000000` → `days=1000000000`; `--a 100000000000000` → `days=1157407407`; `--a 185542587187199` → `days=2147483647`. Message:
```
OverflowError: days=<D>; must have magnitude <= 999999999
```

### 5.4 Tier 1 — `date value out of range` (schedule line 731), forward overflow
`period` is constructible but `datetime.now() + period` exceeds `datetime.max` (9999-12-31 23:59:59.999999). **The boundary is WALL-CLOCK DEPENDENT** ≈ `datetime.max - datetime.now()`; it drifts daily and yearly. **Do not hard-code it.** Measured on 2026-08-10 the largest accepted values were about `a < 2.516e11` s, `b < 4.1936e9` min, `c < 6.9893e7` h — and within one session `--a 251615000000` succeeded while `--a 251615914622` failed. **[RULE]**

Verified Tier-1 cases: `--a 999999999999`; `--b 4294967296`; `--b 250000000000`; `--c 2147483647`; `--c 2147483648`. Note there is **no 32-bit signed cliff** at the argparse/interval level — `--a 2147483647` and `--a 2147483648` both run fine (rc 0); the limit is purely datetime range. **[OBSERVED]**
```
OverflowError: date value out of range
```

### 5.5 Zero interval — non-terminating
`period = timedelta(0)` ⇒ `next_run = now`, and `while next_run <= now: next_run += period` never advances. The process **never terminates**; the `12` line is never reached. Applies to `--a 0`, `--b 0`, `--c 0`, and to every spelling of zero accepted by `int()`: `0`, `-0`, `+0`, `00`, `０`(U+FF10). **[OBSERVED for a and b and c; all zero spellings verified on --a]**
Observable signature on a pipe: rc 124 under `timeout`, **empty stdout, empty stderr**. On a TTY the pre-hang lines appear. Absence of a usage/error block is the proof that `int()` accepted the value — never read "no output" as "rejected". **[RULE]**

Node: implement as a genuinely non-terminating loop (do not exit, do not throw).

### 5.6 Negative interval — Tier 4, walk-back to year 1 (schedule line 734)
A negative interval is **not** rejected: `next_run = now + period` lands in the past, then the loop steps `next_run += period` until the date underflows `datetime.MINYEAR` and raises. rc **1**. **[OBSERVED for `--c`]**
```
OverflowError: date value out of range
```
Iteration count ≈ `(now - datetime.min) / |period|` ≈ `17.76e6 / |hours|` as of 2026-08. Timing model measured on the probe machine: `T ≈ 0.145 s startup + 0.93 s / |hours|` (~52.6 ns per iteration); `|interval| × loop_time` was constant within ~4 % over 1…48 hours (0.935, 0.930, 0.942, 0.924, 0.920, 0.924, 0.936, 0.960). Beyond ~500 h the loop cost vanishes into startup noise. Per-iteration cost is far too small for a clock read inside the loop, so `now` is captured **once** before the loop. **[OBSERVED]**

Consequences for a Node port: the *observable* contract is only `rc 1` + the traceback + the pre-crash stdout. Wall time is machine-specific and need not be reproduced; a direct computation is acceptable. But note the practical hazard: `--b -1` ≈ 56 s and `--a -1` ≈ 3370 s (~56 min) in the reference, so both look like rc 124 under `timeout 8` even though they *do* eventually raise. **[RULE — extrapolated, see UNRESOLVED #1]**

### 5.7 Traceback text (rc 1)

Six lines on stderr, in this order, each LF-terminated, two-space indent on each `File` frame, **no source-echo lines** (the frozen build strips them), relative build paths (`test12.py`, `schedule/__init__.py`), never absolute:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test12.py", line <SRC>, in <module>
  File "schedule/__init__.py", line 657, in do
  File "schedule/__init__.py", line <SCHED>, in _schedule_next_run
OverflowError: <MSG>
[PYI-<pid>:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!
```

Substitutions:

| offending option | `<SRC>` |
|---|---|
| `--a` (seconds) | `11` |
| `--b` (minutes) | `13` |
| `--c` (hours) | `15` |

| regime | `<SCHED>` | `<MSG>` |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 3 | `729` | `Python int too large to convert to C int` |
| Tier 2 | `729` | `days=<D>; must have magnitude <= 999999999` |
| Tier 1 (positive overflow) | `731` | `date value out of range` |
| Tier 4 (negative walk-back) | `734` | `date value out of range` |

`<pid>` is the process id and therefore **changes every run** (`[PYI-523:ERROR]`, `[PYI-1755:ERROR]`, … all observed). Never byte-compare that line; emit `process.pid`. It goes to **stderr, after** the `OverflowError` line. **[RULE]**

Verified full examples: **[OBSERVED]**

```
$ test12_executable --a 5 --b 10 --c -168     # rc 1
stdout: 5\n10\n
stderr:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test12.py", line 15, in <module>
  File "schedule/__init__.py", line 657, in do
  File "schedule/__init__.py", line 734, in _schedule_next_run
OverflowError: date value out of range
[PYI-523:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!
```

```
$ test12_executable --a 999999999999 --b 1 --c 1     # rc 1, stdout EMPTY
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test12.py", line 11, in <module>
  File "schedule/__init__.py", line 657, in do
  File "schedule/__init__.py", line 731, in _schedule_next_run
OverflowError: date value out of range
[PYI-1755:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!
```

```
$ test12_executable --a 1 --b 1 --c 24000000000      # rc 1, stdout "1\n1\n"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test12.py", line 15, in <module>
  File "schedule/__init__.py", line 657, in do
  File "schedule/__init__.py", line 729, in _schedule_next_run
OverflowError: days=1000000000; must have magnitude <= 999999999
[PYI-1578:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!
```

---

## 6. Node implementation notes (zero deps)

1. **BigInt everywhere** for parsed values, `D`, and the tier comparisons. `str(int)` = `BigInt.prototype.toString()` (no separators, no `+`, no leading zeros — matches `print(int)`).
2. **Unicode `Nd` digit value without tables:** `Nd` blocks are contiguous runs of exactly 10 code points starting at the digit-zero. For a code point `cp` matching `/\p{Nd}/u`, walk down at most 9 steps while the predecessor is still `Nd`, stop at the run start `cp0`, then `value = cp - cp0`. Iterate over **code points** (`for (const ch of s)`), not UTF-16 units, so astral digits like `U+1D7DD` work.
3. **`str.isprintable()` in Node:** non-printable ⇔ matches `/[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}\p{Cs}\p{Co}\p{Cn}\p{Zl}\p{Zp}\p{Zs}]/u`, **except** `U+0020` which is printable. Note `\p{Cn}` (unassigned) is supported by V8's property escapes only via `\p{Assigned}` negation — use `/\P{Assigned}/u` for `Cn`.
4. **Error emission helper:** every argparse error is `process.stderr.write(usageLine + "\n" + PROG + ": error: " + detail + "\n")` then `process.exit(2)`; nothing may reach stdout first.
5. **Datetime bounds:** `datetime.min` = 0001-01-01T00:00:00, `datetime.max` = 9999-12-31T23:59:59.999999. JS `Date` cannot represent year 1 through 9999 with microsecond precision safely across the whole span — compute in integer microseconds since a fixed epoch with BigInt rather than with `Date` arithmetic. Tier-1 test: `nowMicros + periodMicros > maxMicros` (forward) or `< minMicros` (backward).
6. **Do not reproduce the timing** of the negative walk-back loop; only rc, stderr, and pre-crash stdout are contractual.
7. **Never invoke the reference binary without a wall-clock timeout** when differential-testing: `0` hangs forever and small negative `--a`/`--b` take minutes. Sleep between runs and use distinct output files — the probes observed a *delayed cross-run stdout flush* from a SIGTERM'd child polluting the next run's capture.

---

## UNRESOLVED

Contradictions, unverified extrapolations, and gaps. None of these are papered over above; each is flagged inline as `[INFERRED]` where used.

1. **Negative intervals: "hangs forever" vs "raises OverflowError after N seconds" — the reports disagree in emphasis, and only `--c` was actually run to completion.**
   Probe 1 rule: "Negative values also parse fine but hang/run very long (`-5` → rc=124, empty stdout+stderr under timeout 8)". Probe 3: "`--a -1` … TIMEOUT (rc=124 at 8s) … per task brief this input takes ~1min+". Probe 4 *did* run negatives to completion but **only for `--c`** (hours), getting rc 1 + line 734. Probe 4 explicitly states it never executed `--a -3600`, `--a -86400`, `--a -1`, `--b -1`, `--b -60`, nor **any** zero case, nor the pipe-vs-tty buffering comparison — all of its statements about those are extrapolations from the fitted model `T = 0.145 + 0.93/|hours|`.
   ⇒ **Unverified:** that negative `--a` and negative `--b` terminate with rc 1 / line 734 at all, and that unit conversion makes cost depend only on absolute period length. The spec's §5.6 negative branch for `--a`/`--b` is inference from `--c`.
2. **A contradictory traceback for `--a=-5`.** Probe 2 recorded one run of `--a=-5 --b 2 --c 3` where a delayed flush produced `OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C int` at **line 729** — which conflicts with Probe 4's line **734** / `date value out of range` for negatives. Probe 2 attributes it to non-deterministic cross-run flushing of a SIGTERM'd child. Not re-verified. If it is real, negative values of large magnitude may hit Tier 3 at 729 before reaching 734 (which §5.1 step 1 would produce, since it tests `|D|`) — but the *specific* value `-5` cannot be Tier 3, so as recorded it is almost certainly contamination.
3. **No probe covered the negative side of Tier 2 / Tier 3 thresholds** (e.g. `--a -185542587187200`, `--c -24000000000`). The `|D|`-based ordering in §5.1 steps 1–2 is inferred by symmetry with `timedelta`'s magnitude check.
4. **Whitespace set is only partially verified.** Confirmed strippable: space, `\t \n \v \f \r`, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000, U+2003, U+3000. Confirmed *not* whitespace: U+200B. Untested: U+001C–U+001F, U+0085, U+2001–U+2002, U+2004–U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F. The spec recommends the full CPython set; a differential test should confirm.
5. **`unit=days` vs `unit=weeks` line count**: not a contradiction, but worth restating because it is easy to get wrong — 8 `weeks` lines, not 7 (`.week` + 7 weekdays), 9 Job lines total.
6. **Which of several bad ints is reported.** Probe 1's note says "`--a` is validated first, so only the first failing flag is ever reported", which conflates *declaration* order with *argv* order. Only `--a 1 --b abc --c 1` was run (both orders agree). A case like `--b x --a y` was never probed, so the "leftmost in argv wins" rule in §2.6 is inferred from argparse's single left-to-right pass.
7. **Help vs. per-option error precedence when help comes *after* a broken option.** Only `--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --help` (all valid) was probed. `--a --help`, `--a= --help`, `--a x --help` are untested, so the position-dependence of the short-circuit is unknown.
8. **Option abbreviation.** argparse defaults to `allow_abbrev=True`. `--ab` was rejected (that is a *suffix/extension*, not an abbreviation) and `--A` is case-mismatched, but a genuine abbreviation of an existing option — `--hel`, `--h`, `--he` for `--help` — was **never probed**. Behaviour is therefore undefined by the probes; do not guess without a differential run.
9. **13 vs 12 stdout lines.** Probe 2's rules text says "Exit code 0 on success (with the 12-line output)" while Probe 1, Probe 3, and every byte-exact baseline capture show **13** lines (3 values + 9 Job + count). Resolved in favour of **13**; Probe 2's "12" is a miscount (it likely refers to the 12 jobs).
10. **Quoting style of the bad-int value.** Probe 2's rule says the value is echoed "with Python repr-style single quotes"; Probe 1 proved with `"5'x"`, `'5\'"x'`, `'5\\x'`, `'\t5x'`, `'5\xa0X'` that it is genuine `repr()` including quote switching. Resolved in favour of **full `repr()`** (§2.7).
11. **JSON transport mangling of two probe cases.** For U+200B, the `stderr` field shows the raw zero-width character while the accompanying note says it is escaped to a `\uNNNN` form; the note is authoritative and consistent with `isprintable()`, so §2.7 specifies `'\u200b5'`. Likewise Probe 3's `--a 12345678901234567890` case omits the `File "schedule/__init__.py", line 657, in do` frame in its `stderr` field but its note states the real block is 6 lines including that frame — the 6-line template in §5.7 is authoritative.
12. **A schema/field inconsistency in Probe 3**: the case `--a 2147483647 --b 2147483647 --c 2147483647` records `exitCode: 0` while its note says "rc was 1, not 0" and its stderr shows the Tier-1 traceback. Treated as **rc 1**.
13. **`surrogateescape` is not reproducible in Node.** Undecodable argv bytes render as `'5\udcff'` in the reference because CPython decodes argv with `surrogateescape`. Node's `process.argv` is decoded as UTF-8 with `U+FFFD` replacement, so lone surrogates are unrecoverable. This is a **known unfixable divergence** for invalid-UTF-8 argv unless the port reads raw argv bytes by another mechanism.
14. **One discarded observation:** Probe 1 saw a fullwidth-zero invocation apparently leave 7 lines of usage text in the stdout capture; three clean re-runs gave empty stdout/stderr with rc 124, so it was ruled a harness artifact. Recorded here in case it reappears.
15. **Tier-1 boundaries are date-dependent and were measured on 2026-08-10** (`a < ~2.516e11`, `b < ~4.1936e9`, `c < ~6.9893e7`). They drift daily and will differ in another year. Never assert them as constants; assert the `now + period > datetime.max` relation instead.
